source_text: SACRAE THEOLOGIAE LIBER SECUNDUS, De fine hominis, ut civis regni Dei, absolute summo & ultimo seu aeterna beatitudine. CAPUT PRIMUM, An detur summum aliquod hominis bonum, idque aeternum & quid sit? Sacrae Theologiae pars communis tria persequitur, finem hominis absolute summum & ultimum, nempe beatitudinem aeternam, subjectum, puta hominem ipsum Dei civem, & principia a quibus dependet salus aeterna, cum mediis, quibus ad eam dirigitur.
english: BOOK TWO. On the end of man, as a citizen of God's kingdom — the absolutely highest and last end, or eternal beatitude.
CHAPTER ONE. Whether there is some highest good of man, and that eternal, and what it is.

The common part of sacred theology pursues three things: the absolutely highest and last end of man, namely eternal beatitude; the subject, that is, man himself as a citizen of God; and the principles on which eternal salvation depends, together with the means by which he is directed to it.

source_text: VII. Immortalitas animae est illius perfectio, qua sine substantiae suae destructione, benignitate creatoris sui in aeternum, durat. Haec opponitur morti stricte sumtae, quatenus est exstinctio, quod ad substantiae destructionem. Ex patribus alioquin quidam mortem laxius accipiunt, pro mutatione quod ad taliter esse, quae demum illa cunque sit. Sic Bernhardus: Omnis, inquit, mutatio mors est. Et ideo Nyssenus probat huic vitae mortem implicatam esse, quod mutationi ista vita subjecta sit. Consentit Augustinus lib. 3. contra Maximinum Arianorum episcopum cap. 12. col. 730. Immortalitatem, inquiens, Deus habere dicitur solus, quia est immutabilis solus. In omni enim mutabili natura nonnulla mors est ipsa mutatio, quia facit aliquid in ea non esse quod erat. Proinde & ipsa anima humana, quae propterea dicitur immortalis, quoniam qualitercunque, secundum modum suum nunquam desinit vivere: habet tamen pro ipso suo modo quandam mortem suam: quia, si juste vivebat & peccat, moritur justitiae: si peccatrix erat & justificatur, moritur peccato: ut alias ejus mutationes taceam, de quibus longum est disputare. Consentit Ambrosius lib. 3. de fide cap. 2. Et anima, inquiens, moritur. Anima enim quae peccaverit, ipsa morietur. Omnis rationabilis creatura accidentia recipit & subjecta judicio est. In accidentibus autem & poena judicii corruptela est & profectus.
english: VII. The immortality of the soul is that perfection of it by which, without destruction of its substance, by the kindness of its Creator, it endures forever.

This is opposed to death strictly taken, inasmuch as it is extinction with respect to the destruction of substance. Otherwise certain of the fathers take death more loosely, for change with respect to being-such, whatever that finally is. So Bernard: Every change, he says, is a death. And therefore Nyssenus proves that death is implicated in this life, because this life is subject to change.

Augustine agrees in book 3 against Maximinus the Arian bishop, chapter 12, column 730: Immortality, he says, God alone is said to have, because he alone is immutable. For in every changeable nature the change itself is some death, because it makes something in it not to be what it was. Accordingly the human soul itself, which is therefore called immortal because in whatever way, according to its own mode, it never ceases to live, nevertheless has according to that same mode a certain death of its own: because if it was living justly and sins, it dies to justice; if it was a sinner and is justified, it dies to sin — not to mention its other changes, about which it is long to dispute.

Ambrose agrees in book 3 On faith, chapter 2: And the soul, he says, dies. For the soul that has sinned, it itself shall die. Every rational creature receives accidents and is subject to judgment. But in accidents both the penalty of judgment is corruption and also progress.

source_text: 2. Est naturae spiritualis. Hoc demonstrant, 1. illius operationes, quae multo nobiliores sunt, quam quae a re corporea proficisci possint. 2. Omnia S. Scripturae loca, quae animam rationalem spiritum appellant, ut Eccl. 12.7. Esa. 26.9. Matth. 27.50. Luc. 23.46. Job. 19.30. Act. 7.60. 1. Cor. 2.11. & 6.20. 2. Cor. 7.1. & Heb. 12.9. Contra Johannem Thessalonicensem episcopum, qui in pseudosynodo Nicena, initio actionis quintae, ad cultum imaginum adstruendum dicere non veretur, Catholicam ecclesiam credere omnem animam esse corpoream: cum multis Stoicae, Italicaeque sectae philosophis, cum Tertulliano & Apollinari quodam Alexandrino, de quo in hist. tripart. lib. 5. cap. 44. & juxta quosdam, Luciferianis, apud August. lib. haeres. cap. 81. Quibus omnibus sanctius sensit concilium tertium Constantinopolitanum, sive oecumenicum sextum, actione undecima: Nascitur, inquiens, Deus humano corpore similiterque & habitu animam rationalem & incorpoream habens. 3. Est separabilis a materia. Nam experientia docet omnes mori. Mors autem nihil aliud est, quam animae a corpore separatio. VI. Est autem hic potissimum consideranda animae rationalis immortalitas, status separationis illius a corpore, carnis resurrectio & quae hanc consequuntur. His enim nondum perspectis & extra dubii aleam positis, summum hominis bonum aeternaque beatitudo plene satis ac distincte doceri nequit.
english: 2. It is of a spiritual nature. This is shown first by its operations, which are far nobler than those that can proceed from a corporeal thing; second by all the places of Holy Scripture that call the rational soul a spirit — as [[Ecclesiastes 12:7>>Eccl. 12:7]]; [[Isaiah 26:9>>Esa. 26:9]]; [[Matthew 27:50>>Matth. 27:50]]; [[Luke 23:46>>Luc. 23:46]]; [[Job 19:30>>Job. 19:30]]; [[Acts 7:60>>Act. 7:60]]; [[1 Corinthians 2:11>>1 Cor. 2:11]] and [[1 Corinthians 6:20>>1 Cor. 6:20]]; [[2 Corinthians 7:1>>2 Cor. 7:1]]; and [[Hebrews 12:9>>Heb. 12:9]].

Against John, bishop of Thessalonica, who in the pseudo-synod of Nicaea, at the beginning of the fifth action, does not fear to say, for establishing the cult of images, that the Catholic Church believes every soul to be corporeal — with many philosophers of the Stoic and Italic sects, with Tertullian and a certain Apollinaris of Alexandria (of whom in the Tripartite History book 5, chapter 44), and according to some with the Luciferians (Augustine, On heresies, chapter 81).

Against all of whom the third Council of Constantinople, or sixth ecumenical, sensed more holy in its eleventh action: God is born, it says, with a human body and likewise with the habit of having a rational and incorporeal soul.
3. It is separable from matter. For experience teaches that all die. But death is nothing other than the separation of the soul from the body.

VI. But here especially is to be considered the immortality of the rational soul, the state of its separation from the body, the resurrection of the flesh, and what follows upon this. For until these are surveyed and set beyond the cast of doubt, the highest good of man and eternal beatitude cannot be taught fully enough and distinctly.

source_text: Haec Thomas, ex quibus simul colligitur, quod & quare homini praeter & ultra naturales scientias, haec supernaturalis doctrina & Theologia sit necessaria, quippe quae veram ipsius praxin, quae secundum pietatem est, evehit & dirigit supra naturam ad summum finem suum & bonum gaudii & gloriae aeternae. Quod bonum luculente satis doceri nequit, nisi aliae hypotheses jam ante in animo lectoris firmatae sint, nimirum, 1. Animae rationalis immortalitas. 2. Ejusdem a corpore suo separatae status. 3. Hujus mundi finis. 4. Resurrectio carnis. 5. Judicium extremum. Quibus recte constitutis, summa regni Dei, hominisque civis hujus regni, beatitudo aliquanto solidius explicabitur.
english: So Thomas. From which it is gathered at once what and why this supernatural doctrine and theology is necessary for man beside and beyond the natural sciences: namely because it raises and directs his true practice — which is according to piety — above nature to his highest end and to the good of eternal joy and glory.

That good cannot be taught clearly enough unless other hypotheses have already been settled in the reader's mind, namely: first, the immortality of the rational soul; second, the state of the same when separated from its body; third, the end of this world; fourth, the resurrection of the flesh; fifth, the last judgment.
When these are rightly established, the highest beatitude of God's kingdom, and of man as citizen of this kingdom, will be explained somewhat more solidly.

source_text: V. Cum itaque homo praeditus sit anima rationali, quae immateriata, indissolubilis & immortalis est, ejusmodi bonum ei convenit, quod mensuram & durationem corporis excedat, & cum ipsa anima immortali post discessum a corpore perennet: quo potita fuerit, felix & beata; sin vero exciderit, extreme misera erit. HOMINI anima rationalis est: id quod tum apud omnes in confesso est, tum ex operationibus animae in nobis omnes experimur. Nam intelligimus, nos e notis in ignotorum notitiam pervenire, quod est ratiocinari. Ex quo colligimus, esse in nobis principium aliquod, a quo operatio isthaec fluat. Hoc vero est anima, quam a tam excellenti effectu rationalem appellamus, de cujus natura hic obiter sequentes regulae observandae sunt.
english: V. Since therefore man is endowed with a rational soul, which is immaterial, indissoluble, and immortal, such a good suits him as exceeds the measure and duration of the body and endures with the immortal soul itself after departure from the body: when he has obtained it he will be happy and blessed; but if he falls from it he will be extremely wretched.

Man has a rational soul: this is confessed among all, and we all experience it from the operations of the soul in us. For we understand that we arrive from known things at knowledge of unknowns, which is to reason.

From which we gather that there is in us some principle from which this operation flows. This is the soul, which from so excellent an effect we call rational; concerning its nature the following rules are to be observed here in passing.
